content.text: Mint an admin token with the recovered secret, then compare a normal object with an admin-only endpoint.

Two issues combine: (1) the HS256 secret `jwtlab2026` is guessable, so any user can forge an admin token; (2) `/api/v1/users/{id}` lacks object-level authorization, so a normal user can read other users. The admin export endpoint returned LAB{cf40268c} and a record count, but no records were downloaded.

content: Write the finding and the remediation plan, including token rotation.

content.text:
**Findings**

| ID | Finding | Severity | CVSS 3.1 | Evidence |
| :-- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| API-1 | Weak JWT signing secret (HS256) | Critical | 9.1 | secret `jwtlab2026` recovered offline |
| API-2 | Broken object-level authorization | High | 7.1 | user can read arbitrary user IDs |
| API-3 | Admin export reachable with forged role | High | 8.1 | export metadata + lab flag |

**Fix:** rotate to a 256-bit random secret stored in a secret manager; pin `alg` to HS256 and reject `none`/algorithm confusion; add an authorization check on every object (`sub` must own the record unless `role=admin`); enforce admin scope server-side, not from the token claim alone; rate-limit login and export. Rotate all tokens issued before the fix.

**Detection:** alert on JWT `alg` changes, tokens with `role=admin` for non-admin subjects, sequential object-ID enumeration, and bulk export calls.

CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-116). `cipher.txt` contains a base64 blob encrypted with
a repeating XOR key (lowercase letters, 4-7 chars). Recover the flag and explain
why this construction is weak.

content.text: Decode the blob, infer the key length from repeating patterns, then recover the key using the known `flag=` prefix.

The repeating XOR key is `sqwjp` and the plaintext is `flag=LAB{010ba241}`. Known-plaintext (`flag=`) plus the short key length makes this recoverable in seconds; XOR also preserves language statistics, so frequency analysis works even without a known prefix.

content: Explain the fix and how to detect weak crypto in code review.

content.text:
**Fix:** use authenticated encryption with a random nonce — AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 — and a key from a KMS/secret manager. Never reuse a nonce with GCM. For password storage, use Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt, not encryption.

**Code-review detection:** grep for `chr(ord(` / `^` loops over data, `base64` used as “encryption”, hard-coded key bytes, `Cipher.getInstance("AES/ECB", ...)`, and `Random()` for keys. Add a SAST rule and a dependency policy for vetted crypto libraries.

00000000000011a9 <check_password>:
    11a9:  endbr64
    11ad:  push   rbp
    11ae:  mov    rbp,rsp
    11b1:  mov    QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8],rdi
    11b5:  mov    rax,QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8]
    11b9:  movzx  eax,BYTE PTR [rax]
    11bc:  xor    eax,0x3d
    11c2:  add    eax,0x3
    11c5:  cmp    al,BYTE PTR [rip+0x2e55]
    11cc:  jne    11e0 <check_password+0x37>
    ...
    11e0:  mov    eax,0x0
    11e5:  pop    rbp
    11e6:  ret
The check transforms each byte as `((c ^ key) + 3)` and compares it to a constant table. Dump the table and invert it in Python.

The comparison is a byte-wise `((input[i] ^ 0x3d) + 3)` against a constant table in `.rodata`. Inverting the transform yields `u"%4q"rr4/30-`. The transform is reversible with the key embedded in the binary, so this is obfuscation, not protection.

content: Confirm the password locally and explain how to fix this design.

content.text: Run the lab binary once with the recovered argument to confirm, then write the design lesson.

Confirmed: `u"%4q"rr4/30-` is accepted and prints LAB{cd3a9adb}. **Fix:** never embed a reusable secret in a client-side binary. Move verification server-side, use a slow password hash (Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt) with a per-user salt, rate-limit attempts, and treat obfuscation as a speed bump only. If the binary must hold a key, use platform secure storage and rotate it.

content.text: Identify protections and look for the comparison routine before brute force.

crackme-45: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, not stripped
    Arch:     amd64-64-little
    RELRO:    Full RELRO
    Stack:    No canary found
    NX:       NX enabled
    PIE:      PIE enabled
    Stripped: No

00000000000011a9 <check_password>:
    11a9:  endbr64
    11ad:  push   rbp
    11ae:  mov    rbp,rsp
    11b1:  mov    QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8],rdi
    11b5:  mov    rax,QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8]
    11b9:  movzx  eax,BYTE PTR [rax]
    11bc:  xor    eax,0x2d
    11c2:  add    eax,0x3
    11c5:  cmp    al,BYTE PTR [rip+0x2e55]
    11cc:  jne    11e0 <check_password+0x37>
    ...
    11e0:  mov    eax,0x0
    11e5:  pop    rbp
    11e6:  ret
The check transforms each byte as `((c ^ key) + 3)` and compares it to a constant table. Dump the table and invert it in Python.

The comparison is a byte-wise `((input[i] ^ 0x2d) + 3)` against a constant table in `.rodata`. Inverting the transform yields `eps$#p$$$>99<`. The transform is reversible with the key embedded in the binary, so this is obfuscation, not protection.

content: Confirm the password locally and explain how to fix this design.

content.text: Run the lab binary once with the recovered argument to confirm, then write the design lesson.

Confirmed: `eps$#p$$$>99<` is accepted and prints LAB{85a0a0b4}. **Fix:** never embed a reusable secret in a client-side binary. Move verification server-side, use a slow password hash (Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt) with a per-user salt, rate-limit attempts, and treat obfuscation as a speed bump only. If the binary must hold a key, use platform secure storage and rotate it.

CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-665). The lab service encrypts `attacker_input + secret` with
AES-128-ECB under a fixed unknown key and returns the ciphertext hex. Recover the secret
using the encryption oracle. The secret is a `LAB{...}` flag.

content.text: ECB encrypts identical 16-byte blocks identically. Confirm the block size and the presence of a repeated block after shifting the input.

A repeated block at 16 and 32 bytes confirms ECB and a 16-byte block size. Use the standard byte-at-a-time attack: align the secret so one unknown byte sits at the end of a block, then match the dictionary.

Recovered `LAB{47d34d63}`. ECB leaks equality: by shifting the input so each unknown byte lands at a known block position, the attacker builds a dictionary of ciphertext blocks and matches them one byte at a time. The attack needs only the encryption oracle.

content: What is the fix, and does adding a random prefix stop the attack?

content.text:
**Fix:** use a randomized AEAD mode (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with a fresh nonce per message. ECB is deterministic and should not be used for anything beyond a single fixed-size block with no attacker influence.

**Random prefix:** it raises the cost but does not stop the attack. The attacker can still locate the secret's block alignment by finding repeated blocks, then apply the same byte-at-a-time technique. It is not a security control; it is at best an obstacle.

content.text:
**Remediation:** do not build a shell string from user input. Use an argument vector (`subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], shell=False)`), validate `host` as an IP or an allowlisted hostname, enforce a destination allowlist, drop capabilities, run in a read-only container, and remove secrets from the web root.

content:
CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-360). The lab service encrypts `attacker_input + secret` with
AES-128-ECB under a fixed unknown key and returns the ciphertext hex. Recover the secret
using the encryption oracle. The secret is a `LAB{...}` flag.

content.text: ECB encrypts identical 16-byte blocks identically. Confirm the block size and the presence of a repeated block after shifting the input.

A repeated block at 16 and 32 bytes confirms ECB and a 16-byte block size. Use the standard byte-at-a-time attack: align the secret so one unknown byte sits at the end of a block, then match the dictionary.

Recovered `LAB{899c7e9a}`. ECB leaks equality: by shifting the input so each unknown byte lands at a known block position, the attacker builds a dictionary of ciphertext blocks and matches them one byte at a time. The attack needs only the encryption oracle.

content: What is the fix, and does adding a random prefix stop the attack?

content.text:
**Fix:** use a randomized AEAD mode (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with a fresh nonce per message. ECB is deterministic and should not be used for anything beyond a single fixed-size block with no attacker influence.

**Random prefix:** it raises the cost but does not stop the attack. The attacker can still locate the secret's block alignment by finding repeated blocks, then apply the same byte-at-a-time technique. It is not a security control; it is at best an obstacle.

content.text:
**Remediation:** do not build a shell string from user input. **Remediation:** do not build a shell string from user input. Use an argument vector (`subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], shell=False)`), validate `host` as an IP or an allowlisted hostname, enforce a destination allowlist, drop capabilities, run in a read-only container, and remove secrets from the web root.

00000000000011a9 <check_password>:
    11a9:  endbr64
    11ad:  push   rbp
    11ae:  mov    rbp,rsp
    11b1:  mov    QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8],rdi

    11bc:  xor    eax,0x79
    11c2:  add    eax,0x3
    11c5:  cmp    al,BYTE PTR [rip+0x2e55]
    11cc:  jne    11e0 <check_password+0x37>
    ...
    11e0:  mov    eax,0x0
    11e5:  pop    rbp
    11e6:  ret
The check transforms each byte as `((c ^ key) + 3)` and compares it to a constant table. Dump the table and invert it in Python.

The comparison is a byte-wise `((input[i] ^ 0x79) + 3)` against a constant table in `.rodata`. Inverting the transform yields `9<?x-<..xrmrs`. The transform is reversible with the key embedded in the binary, so this is obfuscation, not protection.

content: Confirm the password locally and explain how to fix this design.

content.text: Run the lab binary once with the recovered argument to confirm, then write the design lesson.

Confirmed: `9<?x-<..xrmrs` is accepted and prints LAB{4cd66378}. **Fix:** never embed a reusable secret in a client-side binary. Move verification server-side, use a slow password hash (Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt) with a per-user salt, rate-limit attempts, and treat obfuscation as a speed bump only. If the binary must hold a key, use platform secure storage and rotate it.

password. It is a lab binary; do not run it against any service. Reading, disassembly,
and local execution with the recovered argument are allowed.

content.text: Identify protections and look for the comparison routine before brute force.

crackme-87: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, not stripped
    Arch:     amd64-64-little
    RELRO:    Full RELRO
    Stack:    No canary found
    NX:       NX enabled
    PIE:      PIE enabled
    Stripped: No

00000000000011a9 <check_password>:
    11a9:  endbr64
    11ad:  push   rbp
    11ae:  mov    rbp,rsp
    11b1:  mov    QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8],rdi
    11b5:  mov    rax,QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8]
    11b9:  movzx  eax,BYTE PTR [rax]
    11bc:  xor    eax,0x3b
    11c2:  add    eax,0x3
    11c5:  cmp    al,BYTE PTR [rip+0x2e55]
    11cc:  jne    11e0 <check_password+0x37>
    ...
    11e0:  mov    eax,0x0
    11e5:  pop    rbp
    11e6:  ret
The check transforms each byte as `((c ^ key) + 3)` and compares it to a constant table. Dump the table and invert it in Python.

The comparison is a byte-wise `((input[i] ^ 0x3b) + 3)` against a constant table in `.rodata`. Inverting the transform yields `{~}:o~ll:'.32`. The transform is reversible with the key embedded in the binary, so this is obfuscation, not protection.

content: Confirm the password locally and explain how to fix this design.

content.text: Run the lab binary once with the recovered argument to confirm, then write the design lesson.

Confirmed: `{~}:o~ll:'.32` is accepted and prints LAB{21ecd4d2}. **Fix:** never embed a reusable secret in a client-side binary. Move verification server-side, use a slow password hash (Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt) with a per-user salt, rate-limit attempts, and treat obfuscation as a speed bump only. If the binary must hold a key, use platform secure storage and rotate it.

Engagement ENG-2026-691 — authorized test of http://ci.lab.local (192.0.2.41).
`/fetch?url=` proxies a user-supplied URL. Determine whether it can reach internal
services (SSRF), read-only. Do not fetch customer data or use any credentials found.

content.text: Baseline the proxy with a documented internal health endpoint, then test loopback and link-local.
The request failed to connect. That could be a transient gateway hiccup or a rate limiter; retry once with the normal timeout before changing the payload.

Error (28):
curl: (28) Failed to connect after 8001 ms: Couldn't connect to server
The retry completed; continue with the original plan and treat the first failure as transport noise.
Loopback works. Test the cloud metadata endpoint next, but only read identity metadata.

SSRF is confirmed: the proxy can reach loopback (192.0.2.5:8081) and the cloud metadata service. AWS IMDSv1 is reachable and returns temporary role credentials for `web-prod-role`. The proxy returned the response body to an unauthenticated caller. I did not use the credentials; the impact is proven by the token response.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** temporary AWS credentials for the web tier's instance role; blast radius depends on that role. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** enforce IMDSv2 (token-required), scope the instance role to the reporting bucket prefix, add egress controls, and block link-local destinations at the application layer.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

content:
CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-575). The lab service encrypts `attacker_input + secret` with
AES-128-ECB under a fixed unknown key and returns the ciphertext hex. Recover the secret
using the encryption oracle. The secret is a `LAB{...}` flag.

content.text: ECB encrypts identical 16-byte blocks identically. Confirm the block size and the presence of a repeated block after shifting the input.

A repeated block at 16 and 32 bytes confirms ECB and a 16-byte block size. Use the standard byte-at-a-time attack: align the secret so one unknown byte sits at the end of a block, then match the dictionary.

Recovered `LAB{8eed7ac9}`. ECB leaks equality: by shifting the input so each unknown byte lands at a known block position, the attacker builds a dictionary of ciphertext blocks and matches them one byte at a time. The attack needs only the encryption oracle.

content: What is the fix, and does adding a random prefix stop the attack?

content.text:
**Fix:** use a randomized AEAD mode (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with a fresh nonce per message. ECB is deterministic and should not be used for anything beyond a single fixed-size block with no attacker influence.

**Random prefix:** it raises the cost but does not stop the attack. The attacker can still locate the secret's block alignment by finding repeated blocks, then apply the same byte-at-a-time technique. It is not a security control; it is at best an obstacle.

Engagement ENG-2026-612 — authorized test of http://api.lab.local (10.20.30.160).
`/fetch?url=` proxies a user-supplied URL. Determine whether it can reach internal
services (SSRF), read-only. Do not fetch customer data or use any credentials found.

content.text: Baseline the proxy with a documented internal health endpoint, then test loopback and link-local.
Loopback works. Test the cloud metadata endpoint next, but only read identity metadata.

SSRF is confirmed: the proxy can reach loopback (10.20.30.2:8081) and the cloud metadata service. The GCE metadata server is reachable and returns the default service-account token. The proxy returned the response body to an unauthenticated caller. I did not use the credentials; the impact is proven by the token response.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** a GCP access token for the instance's default service account. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** block metadata.google.internal and 169.254.169.254, require the Metadata-Flavor header at the proxy, and remove the default service account from the instance.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

CTF reverse-engineering task (ENG-2026-215). Analyze `crackme-96` and recover the accepted
password. It is a lab binary; do not run it against any service. Reading, disassembly,
and local execution with the recovered argument are allowed.

content.text: Identify protections and look for the comparison routine before brute force.

crackme-96: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, not stripped
    Arch:     amd64-64-little
    RELRO:    Full RELRO
    Stack:    No canary found
    NX:       NX enabled
    PIE:      PIE enabled
    Stripped: No

00000000000011a9 <check_password>:
    11a9:  endbr64
    11ad:  push   rbp
    11ae:  mov    rbp,rsp
    11b1:  mov    QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8],rdi
    11b5:  mov    rax,QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8]
    11b9:  movzx  eax,BYTE PTR [rax]
    11bc:  xor    eax,0x62
    11c2:  add    eax,0x3
    11c5:  cmp    al,BYTE PTR [rip+0x2e55]
    11cc:  jne    11e0 <check_password+0x37>
    ...
    11e0:  mov    eax,0x0
    11e5:  pop    rbp
    11e6:  ret
The check transforms each byte as `((c ^ key) + 3)` and compares it to a constant table. Dump the table and invert it in Python.

The comparison is a byte-wise `((input[i] ^ 0x62) + 3)` against a constant table in `.rodata`. Inverting the transform yields `2'$s6'55s{y~y`. The transform is reversible with the key embedded in the binary, so this is obfuscation, not protection.

content: Confirm the password locally and explain how to fix this design.

content.text: Run the lab binary once with the recovered argument to confirm, then write the design lesson.

Confirmed: `2'$s6'55s{y~y` is accepted and prints LAB{113ebdde}. **Fix:** never embed a reusable secret in a client-side binary. Move verification server-side, use a slow password hash (Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt) with a per-user salt, rate-limit attempts, and treat obfuscation as a speed bump only. If the binary must hold a key, use platform secure storage and rotate it.

The request failed to connect. That could be a transient gateway hiccup or a rate limiter; retry once with the normal timeout before changing the payload.

Error (28):
curl: (28) Failed to connect after 8001 ms: Couldn't connect to server
The retry completed; continue with the original plan and treat the first failure as transport noise.
Loopback works. Test the cloud metadata endpoint next, but only read identity metadata.

SSRF is confirmed: the proxy can reach loopback (192.0.2.9:8081) and the cloud metadata service. The GCE metadata server is reachable and returns the default service-account token. The proxy returned the response body to an unauthenticated caller. I did not use the credentials; the impact is proven by the token response.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** a GCP access token for the instance's default service account. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** block metadata.google.internal and 169.254.169.254, require the Metadata-Flavor header at the proxy, and remove the default service account from the instance.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

content.text: Order actions by blast radius and preserve evidence before eradication.

CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-532). `cipher.txt` contains a base64 blob encrypted with
a repeating XOR key (lowercase letters, 4-7 chars). Recover the flag and explain
why this construction is weak.

content.text: Decode the blob, infer the key length from repeating patterns, then recover the key using the known `flag=` prefix.

The repeating XOR key is `fmmved` and the plaintext is `flag=LAB{53c00a59}`. Known-plaintext (`flag=`) plus the short key length makes this recoverable in seconds; XOR also preserves language statistics, so frequency analysis works even without a known prefix.

content: Explain the fix and how to detect weak crypto in code review.

content.text:
**Fix:** use authenticated encryption with a random nonce — AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 — and a key from a KMS/secret manager. Never reuse a nonce with GCM. For password storage, use Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt, not encryption.

**Code-review detection:** grep for `chr(ord(` / `^` loops over data, `base64` used as “encryption”, hard-coded key bytes, `Cipher.getInstance("AES/ECB", ...)`, and `Random()` for keys. Add a SAST rule and a dependency policy for vetted crypto libraries.

content.text: Map the static capabilities to host and network detections, then outline containment.

**Detection**

```yara
rule Lab_Linux_Dropper {
    meta:
        author = "mesosfer lab"
        description = "Detects the lab dropper by C2 string and hidden staging path"
        severity = "high"
    strings:
```
        $c2 = "cdn-sync.lab.local" ascii wide
        $stage = "/dev/shm/.cache" ascii
        $ua = "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) lab" ascii
    condition:

- Network: DNS/TLS SNI to `cdn-sync.lab.local` and POSTs to `/api/gate` from servers that should not talk to that domain.
- Host: new cron entries in `/etc/cron.d` or per-user crontabs; files under `/dev/shm`, `/var/tmp`, `/tmp` with the ELF magic and the staging-path string; `crontab` spawned by a web/app process.

**IR steps:** isolate the host, capture volatile data, remove the cron persistence, delete the staged binary after hashing it, block the C2, rotate credentials used on the host, and scan the fleet with the YARA rule. Do not run the sample outside the malware lab.

crackme-36: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, not stripped
    Arch:     amd64-64-little

00000000000011a9 <check_password>:
    11a9:  endbr64
    11ad:  push   rbp
    11ae:  mov    rbp,rsp
    11b1:  mov    QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8],rdi
    11b5:  mov    rax,QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8]

The check transforms each byte as `((c ^ key) + 3)` and compares it to a constant table. Dump the table and invert it in Python.

The comparison is a byte-wise `((input[i] ^ 0x3c) + 3)` against a constant table in `.rodata`. Inverting the transform yields `t#$5p#ss5.220`. The transform is reversible with the key embedded in the binary, so this is obfuscation, not protection.

content.text:
**Remediation:** do not build a shell string from user input. Use an argument vector (`subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], shell=False)`), validate `host` as an IP or an allowlisted hostname, enforce a destination allowlist, drop capabilities, run in a read-only container, and remove secrets from the web root.

CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-844). The lab service encrypts `attacker_input + secret` with
AES-128-ECB under a fixed unknown key and returns the ciphertext hex. Recover the secret
using the encryption oracle. The secret is a `LAB{...}` flag.

content.text: ECB encrypts identical 16-byte blocks identically. Confirm the block size and the presence of a repeated block after shifting the input.

A repeated block at 16 and 32 bytes confirms ECB and a 16-byte block size. Use the standard byte-at-a-time attack: align the secret so one unknown byte sits at the end of a block, then match the dictionary.

Recovered `LAB{00e8c059}`. ECB leaks equality: by shifting the input so each unknown byte lands at a known block position, the attacker builds a dictionary of ciphertext blocks and matches them one byte at a time. The attack needs only the encryption oracle.

content: What is the fix, and does adding a random prefix stop the attack?

content.text:
**Fix:** use a randomized AEAD mode (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with a fresh nonce per message. ECB is deterministic and should not be used for anything beyond a single fixed-size block with no attacker influence.

**Random prefix:** it raises the cost but does not stop the attack. The attacker can still locate the secret's block alignment by finding repeated blocks, then apply the same byte-at-a-time technique. It is not a security control; it is at best an obstacle.

content: Explain the fix and how to detect weak crypto in code review.

content.text:

The request failed to connect. That could be a transient gateway hiccup or a rate limiter; retry once with the normal timeout before changing the payload.

Error (28):
curl: (28) Failed to connect after 8001 ms: Couldn't connect to server
The retry completed; continue with the original plan and treat the first failure as transport noise.
Loopback works. Test the cloud metadata endpoint next, but only read identity metadata.

SSRF is confirmed: the proxy can reach loopback (192.0.2.7:8081) and the cloud metadata service. The GCE metadata server is reachable and returns the default service-account token. The proxy returned the response body to an unauthenticated caller. I did not use the credentials; the impact is proven by the token response.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** a GCP access token for the instance's default service account. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** block metadata.google.internal and 169.254.169.254, require the Metadata-Flavor header at the proxy, and remove the default service account from the instance.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

content: Give the remediation and a detection rule. Also explain why input filtering alone fails.

content.text:
**Remediation:** do not build a shell string from user input. Use an argument vector (`subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], shell=False)`), validate `host` as an IP or an allowlisted hostname, enforce a destination allowlist, drop capabilities, run in a read-only container, and remove secrets from the web root.

**Why filtering fails:** blocklists miss newline, `$IFS`, backticks, Unicode, and argument-injection variants; the underlying shell still interprets whatever survives. Removing the shell is the only reliable fix.

**Detection:** alert on shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `&`, `$`, backticks, `%0a`) in `host`; correlate with child processes of the web server (`ping`, `sh`, `id`, `cat`) and with reads of `/etc/passwd` or `/var/www/**/flag*`.

content.text: Baseline the proxy with a documented internal health endpoint, then test loopback and link-local.
Loopback works. Test the cloud metadata endpoint next, but only read identity metadata.

SSRF is confirmed: the proxy can reach loopback (172.16.20.5:8081) and the cloud metadata service. The GCE metadata server is reachable and returns the default service-account token. The proxy returned the response body to an unauthenticated caller. I did not use the credentials; the impact is proven by the token response.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** a GCP access token for the instance's default service account. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** block metadata.google.internal and 169.254.169.254, require the Metadata-Flavor header at the proxy, and remove the default service account from the instance.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** a GCP access token for the instance's default service account. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** block metadata.google.internal and 169.254.169.254, require the Metadata-Flavor header at the proxy, and remove the default service account from the instance.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

Engagement ENG-2026-787 — authorized test of http://billing.lab.local (172.16.20.54).
`/fetch?url=` proxies a user-supplied URL. Determine whether it can reach internal
services (SSRF), read-only. Do not fetch customer data or use any credentials found.

content.text: Baseline the proxy with a documented internal health endpoint, then test loopback and link-local.
Loopback works. Test the cloud metadata endpoint next, but only read identity metadata.

SSRF is confirmed: the proxy can reach loopback (172.16.20.8:8081) and the cloud metadata service. The GCE metadata server is reachable and returns the default service-account token. The proxy returned the response body to an unauthenticated caller. I did not use the credentials; the impact is proven by the token response.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** a GCP access token for the instance's default service account. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** block metadata.google.internal and 169.254.169.254, require the Metadata-Flavor header at the proxy, and remove the default service account from the instance.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

content.text: Map the static capabilities to host and network detections, then outline containment.

**Detection**

```yara
rule Lab_Linux_Dropper {
    meta:
        author = "mesosfer lab"
        description = "Detects the lab dropper by C2 string and hidden staging path"
        severity = "high"
    strings:
```

CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-784). The lab service encrypts `attacker_input + secret` with
AES-128-ECB under a fixed unknown key and returns the ciphertext hex. Recover the secret
using the encryption oracle. The secret is a `LAB{...}` flag.

content.text: ECB encrypts identical 16-byte blocks identically. Confirm the block size and the presence of a repeated block after shifting the input.

A repeated block at 16 and 32 bytes confirms ECB and a 16-byte block size. Use the standard byte-at-a-time attack: align the secret so one unknown byte sits at the end of a block, then match the dictionary.

Recovered `LAB{07e3a513}`. ECB leaks equality: by shifting the input so each unknown byte lands at a known block position, the attacker builds a dictionary of ciphertext blocks and matches them one byte at a time. The attack needs only the encryption oracle.

content: What is the fix, and does adding a random prefix stop the attack?

content.text:
**Fix:** use a randomized AEAD mode (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with a fresh nonce per message. ECB is deterministic and should not be used for anything beyond a single fixed-size block with no attacker influence.

**Random prefix:** it raises the cost but does not stop the attack. The attacker can still locate the secret's block alignment by finding repeated blocks, then apply the same byte-at-a-time technique. It is not a security control; it is at best an obstacle.

CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-880). The lab service encrypts `attacker_input + secret` with
AES-128-ECB under a fixed unknown key and returns the ciphertext hex. Recover the secret
using the encryption oracle. The secret is a `LAB{...}` flag.

content.text: ECB encrypts identical 16-byte blocks identically. Confirm the block size and the presence of a repeated block after shifting the input.

A repeated block at 16 and 32 bytes confirms ECB and a 16-byte block size. Use the standard byte-at-a-time attack: align the secret so one unknown byte sits at the end of a block, then match the dictionary.

Recovered `LAB{9787edf2}`. ECB leaks equality: by shifting the input so each unknown byte lands at a known block position, the attacker builds a dictionary of ciphertext blocks and matches them one byte at a time. The attack needs only the encryption oracle.

content: What is the fix, and does adding a random prefix stop the attack?

content.text:
**Fix:** use a randomized AEAD mode (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with a fresh nonce per message. ECB is deterministic and should not be used for anything beyond a single fixed-size block with no attacker influence.

**Random prefix:** it raises the cost but does not stop the attack. The attacker can still locate the secret's block alignment by finding repeated blocks, then apply the same byte-at-a-time technique. It is not a security control; it is at best an obstacle.

content.text: Map the static capabilities to host and network detections, then outline containment.

```yara
rule Lab_Linux_Dropper {

        author = "mesosfer lab"
        description = "Detects the lab dropper by C2 string and hidden staging path"
        severity = "high"
    strings:
```

content: Explain the fix and how to detect weak crypto in code review.

content: Write the finding and the remediation plan, including token rotation.

content.text:
**Findings**

| ID | Finding | Severity | CVSS 3.1 | Evidence |
| :-- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| API-1 | Weak JWT signing secret (HS256) | Critical | 9.1 | secret `supersecret` recovered offline |
| API-2 | Broken object-level authorization | High | 7.1 | user can read arbitrary user IDs |
| API-3 | Admin export reachable with forged role | High | 8.1 | export metadata + lab flag |

content.text:
**Remediation:** do not build a shell string from user input. content.text: Map the static capabilities to host and network detections, then outline containment.

**Detection**

```yara
rule Lab_Linux_Dropper {
    meta:
        author = "mesosfer lab"
        description = "Detects the lab dropper by C2 string and hidden staging path"
        severity = "high"
    strings:
        $c2 = "cdn-sync.lab.local" ascii wide
```

- Network: DNS/TLS SNI to `cdn-sync.lab.local` and POSTs to `/api/gate` from servers that should not talk to that domain.
- Host: new cron entries in `/etc/cron.d` or per-user crontabs; files under `/dev/shm`, `/var/tmp`, `/tmp` with the ELF magic and the staging-path string; `crontab` spawned by a web/app process.
- EDR: process lineage `www-data → sh → crontab`, `setsid` from a web process, and outbound connections to the C2.

**IR steps:** isolate the host, capture volatile data, remove the cron persistence, delete the staged binary after hashing it, block the C2, rotate credentials used on the host, and scan the fleet with the YARA rule. Do not run the sample outside the malware lab.

content:
CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-420). The lab service encrypts `attacker_input + secret` with
AES-128-ECB under a fixed unknown key and returns the ciphertext hex. Recover the secret
using the encryption oracle. The secret is a `LAB{...}` flag.

content.text: ECB encrypts identical 16-byte blocks identically. Confirm the block size and the presence of a repeated block after shifting the input.

A repeated block at 16 and 32 bytes confirms ECB and a 16-byte block size. Use the standard byte-at-a-time attack: align the secret so one unknown byte sits at the end of a block, then match the dictionary.

Recovered `LAB{51dc3a8e}`. ECB leaks equality: by shifting the input so each unknown byte lands at a known block position, the attacker builds a dictionary of ciphertext blocks and matches them one byte at a time. The attack needs only the encryption oracle.

content: What is the fix, and does adding a random prefix stop the attack?

content.text:
**Fix:** use a randomized AEAD mode (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with a fresh nonce per message. ECB is deterministic and should not be used for anything beyond a single fixed-size block with no attacker influence.

**Random prefix:** it raises the cost but does not stop the attack. The attacker can still locate the secret's block alignment by finding repeated blocks, then apply the same byte-at-a-time technique. It is not a security control; it is at best an obstacle.

The request failed to connect. That could be a transient gateway hiccup or a rate limiter; retry once with the normal timeout before changing the payload.

Error (28):
curl: (28) Failed to connect after 8001 ms: Couldn't connect to server
The retry completed; continue with the original plan and treat the first failure as transport noise.
Loopback works. Test the cloud metadata endpoint next, but only read identity metadata.

SSRF is confirmed: the proxy can reach loopback (10.20.30.3:8081) and the cloud metadata service. The GCE metadata server is reachable and returns the default service-account token. The proxy returned the response body to an unauthenticated caller. I did not use the credentials; the impact is proven by the token response.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** a GCP access token for the instance's default service account. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** block metadata.google.internal and 169.254.169.254, require the Metadata-Flavor header at the proxy, and remove the default service account from the instance.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

Engagement ENG-2026-482 — authorized test of http://files.lab.local (10.20.30.49).
`/fetch?url=` proxies a user-supplied URL. Determine whether it can reach internal
services (SSRF), read-only. Do not fetch customer data or use any credentials found.

content.text: Baseline the proxy with a documented internal health endpoint, then test loopback and link-local.
Loopback works. Test the cloud metadata endpoint next, but only read identity metadata.

SSRF is confirmed: the proxy can reach loopback (10.20.30.8:8081) and the cloud metadata service. The managed identity token endpoint is reachable through the proxy. The proxy returned the response body to an unauthenticated caller. I did not use the credentials; the impact is proven by the token response.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** a managed identity token for the web VM, usable against the Azure control plane within its RBAC scope. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** require `Metadata: true` at the proxy, block 169.254.169.254/32 for application egress, and reduce the managed identity to the minimum role assignment.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

content.text: Map the static capabilities to host and network detections, then outline containment.

**Detection**

```yara
rule Lab_Linux_Dropper {
    meta:
        author = "mesosfer lab"
        description = "Detects the lab dropper by C2 string and hidden staging path"
        severity = "high"
    strings:
        $c2 = "cdn-sync.lab.local" ascii wide

        $ua = "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) lab" ascii
    condition:
        uint32(0) == 0x464c457f and 2 of them
}
```

- Network: DNS/TLS SNI to `cdn-sync.lab.local` and POSTs to `/api/gate` from servers that should not talk to that domain.
- Host: new cron entries in `/etc/cron.d` or per-user crontabs; files under `/dev/shm`, `/var/tmp`, `/tmp` with the ELF magic and the staging-path string; `crontab` spawned by a web/app process.
- EDR: process lineage `www-data → sh → crontab`, `setsid` from a web process, and outbound connections to the C2.

**IR steps:** isolate the host, capture volatile data, remove the cron persistence, delete the staged binary after hashing it, block the C2, rotate credentials used on the host, and scan the fleet with the YARA rule. Do not run the sample outside the malware lab.

The engine evaluates expressions and string multiplication, which confirms SSTI rather than reflected text. Prove code execution with `id` only.

SSTI is confirmed in the `name` parameter (Freemarker). The arithmetic probe returned 49, string multiplication returned 7777777 (so this is template evaluation, not client-side), and a benign `id` executed as `www-data`. An attacker can run arbitrary commands in the template context.

Use logic-less templates or a strict sandbox (Jinja2 `SandboxedEnvironment`, Twig sandbox extension, Freemarker `TemplateClassResolver.SAFER_RESOLVER`), pass user data as variables, and keep template editing behind an authenticated admin role. **Detection:** alert on template delimiters in user-controlled parameters and on child processes spawned by the app server (`sh`, `id`, `cat`).

content: Give the remediation and a detection rule. Also explain why input filtering alone fails.

content.text:
**Remediation:** do not build a shell string from user input. Use an argument vector (`subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], shell=False)`), validate `host` as an IP or an allowlisted hostname, enforce a destination allowlist, drop capabilities, run in a read-only container, and remove secrets from the web root.

**Why filtering fails:** blocklists miss newline, `$IFS`, backticks, Unicode, and argument-injection variants; the underlying shell still interprets whatever survives. Removing the shell is the only reliable fix.

**Detection:** alert on shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `&`, `$`, backticks, `%0a`) in `host`; correlate with child processes of the web server (`ping`, `sh`, `id`, `cat`) and with reads of `/etc/passwd` or `/var/www/**/flag*`.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** a managed identity token for the web VM, usable against the Azure control plane within its RBAC scope. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** require `Metadata: true` at the proxy, block 169.254.169.254/32 for application egress, and reduce the managed identity to the minimum role assignment.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

content: Give the remediation and a detection rule. Also explain why input filtering alone fails.

content.text:
**Remediation:** do not build a shell string from user input. content:
CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-486). The lab service encrypts `attacker_input + secret` with
AES-128-ECB under a fixed unknown key and returns the ciphertext hex. Recover the secret
using the encryption oracle. The secret is a `LAB{...}` flag.

content.text: ECB encrypts identical 16-byte blocks identically. Confirm the block size and the presence of a repeated block after shifting the input.

A repeated block at 16 and 32 bytes confirms ECB and a 16-byte block size. Use the standard byte-at-a-time attack: align the secret so one unknown byte sits at the end of a block, then match the dictionary.

Recovered `LAB{24f62acb}`. ECB leaks equality: by shifting the input so each unknown byte lands at a known block position, the attacker builds a dictionary of ciphertext blocks and matches them one byte at a time. The attack needs only the encryption oracle.

content: What is the fix, and does adding a random prefix stop the attack?

content.text:
**Fix:** use a randomized AEAD mode (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with a fresh nonce per message. ECB is deterministic and should not be used for anything beyond a single fixed-size block with no attacker influence.

**Random prefix:** it raises the cost but does not stop the attack. The attacker can still locate the secret's block alignment by finding repeated blocks, then apply the same byte-at-a-time technique. It is not a security control; it is at best an obstacle.

CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-575). `cipher.txt` contains a base64 blob encrypted with
a repeating XOR key (lowercase letters, 4-7 chars). Recover the flag and explain
why this construction is weak.

content.text: Decode the blob, infer the key length from repeating patterns, then recover the key using the known `flag=` prefix.

The repeating XOR key is `umxey` and the plaintext is `flag=LAB{f4591b86}`. Known-plaintext (`flag=`) plus the short key length makes this recoverable in seconds; XOR also preserves language statistics, so frequency analysis works even without a known prefix.

content: Explain the fix and how to detect weak crypto in code review.

content.text:
**Fix:** use authenticated encryption with a random nonce — AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 — and a key from a KMS/secret manager. Never reuse a nonce with GCM. For password storage, use Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt, not encryption.

**Code-review detection:** grep for `chr(ord(` / `^` loops over data, `base64` used as “encryption”, hard-coded key bytes, `Cipher.getInstance("AES/ECB", ...)`, and `Random()` for keys. Add a SAST rule and a dependency policy for vetted crypto libraries.

    Arch:     amd64-64-little
    RELRO:    Full RELRO

00000000000011a9 <check_password>:
    11a9:  endbr64
    11ad:  push   rbp
    11ae:  mov    rbp,rsp
    11b1:  mov    QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8],rdi
    11b5:  mov    rax,QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8]
    11b9:  movzx  eax,BYTE PTR [rax]
    11bc:  xor    eax,0x38
    11c2:  add    eax,0x3
    11c5:  cmp    al,BYTE PTR [rip+0x2e55]
    11cc:  jne    11e0 <check_password+0x37>
    ...
    11e0:  mov    eax,0x0
    11e5:  pop    rbp
    11e6:  ret
The check transforms each byte as `((c ^ key) + 3)` and compares it to a constant table. Dump the table and invert it in Python.

The comparison is a byte-wise `((input[i] ^ 0x38) + 3)` against a constant table in `.rodata`. Inverting the transform yields `x}~9l}oo9./10`. The transform is reversible with the key embedded in the binary, so this is obfuscation, not protection.

content: Confirm the password locally and explain how to fix this design.

content.text: Run the lab binary once with the recovered argument to confirm, then write the design lesson.

Confirmed: `x}~9l}oo9./10` is accepted and prints LAB{ed951bcc}. **Fix:** never embed a reusable secret in a client-side binary. content:
CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-120). The lab service encrypts `attacker_input + secret` with
AES-128-ECB under a fixed unknown key and returns the ciphertext hex. Recover the secret
using the encryption oracle. The secret is a `LAB{...}` flag.

content.text: ECB encrypts identical 16-byte blocks identically. Confirm the block size and the presence of a repeated block after shifting the input.

A repeated block at 16 and 32 bytes confirms ECB and a 16-byte block size. Use the standard byte-at-a-time attack: align the secret so one unknown byte sits at the end of a block, then match the dictionary.

Recovered `LAB{db40076b}`. ECB leaks equality: by shifting the input so each unknown byte lands at a known block position, the attacker builds a dictionary of ciphertext blocks and matches them one byte at a time. The attack needs only the encryption oracle.

content: What is the fix, and does adding a random prefix stop the attack?

content.text:
**Fix:** use a randomized AEAD mode (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with a fresh nonce per message. ECB is deterministic and should not be used for anything beyond a single fixed-size block with no attacker influence.

**Random prefix:** it raises the cost but does not stop the attack. The attacker can still locate the secret's block alignment by finding repeated blocks, then apply the same byte-at-a-time technique. It is not a security control; it is at best an obstacle.

SSRF is confirmed: the proxy can reach loopback (10.10.14.6:8081) and the cloud metadata service. The managed identity token endpoint is reachable through the proxy. The proxy returned the response body to an unauthenticated caller. I did not use the credentials; the impact is proven by the token response.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** a managed identity token for the web VM, usable against the Azure control plane within its RBAC scope. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** require `Metadata: true` at the proxy, block 169.254.169.254/32 for application egress, and reduce the managed identity to the minimum role assignment.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

**Detection:** normalize and inspect file-related parameters for `..`, `%2e%2e`, `%252e`, backslashes, and absolute paths; alert when a 200 response resolves outside the document root. Correlate with reads of `/etc/passwd`, `.env`, `id_rsa`, and cloud credential files.

**Residual risk:** even after path allowlisting, symlinks inside the allowed directory can escape it. Resolve the final path and verify it is still under the base directory; disable follow-symlinks in the file server. Rotate the DB password seen in `.env` regardless of the fix.

Command injection confirmed: the `host` value is passed to a shell. Commands run as `www-data` on `lab-web-01`, and the lab flag is readable. This is remote code execution without authentication.

content: Give the remediation and a detection rule. Also explain why input filtering alone fails.

content.text:
**Remediation:** do not build a shell string from user input. Use an argument vector (`subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], shell=False)`), validate `host` as an IP or an allowlisted hostname, enforce a destination allowlist, drop capabilities, run in a read-only container, and remove secrets from the web root.

**Why filtering fails:** blocklists miss newline, `$IFS`, backticks, Unicode, and argument-injection variants; the underlying shell still interprets whatever survives. Removing the shell is the only reliable fix.

**Detection:** alert on shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `&`, `$`, backticks, `%0a`) in `host`; correlate with child processes of the web server (`ping`, `sh`, `id`, `cat`) and with reads of `/etc/passwd` or `/var/www/**/flag*`.

content: Propose containment, eradication, and the detections that would have caught this earlier.

content.text: Order actions by blast radius and preserve evidence before eradication.

**Containment (in order)**
1. Isolate `lab-app-90` from the network; preserve memory and logs first.
2. Disable `svc_backup` and revoke its sessions/keys; force a password reset and check for reuse on other hosts.
3. Block `203.0.113.60` and `update.lab.local` at egress/proxy; preserve the exported file hash.
4. Remove the cron entry and the staged `/tmp/export.csv` after hashing.

**Eradication/recovery**
- Reimage if persistence cannot be fully enumerated; otherwise remove cron/systemd units, rotate credentials, and verify no new SSH keys or users.
- Review the export contents and notify the data owner.

**Detection that should have fired**
- ≥10 failed SSH logins per source in 5 minutes, then a success from the same source.
- Admin export download >5 MB or a new export by a non-admin account.
- `curl`/`wget` POSTs from an app host to a newly observed domain, especially with a file argument (`-d @`).
- `crontab -` modification by a service account, and `curl` in a cron line.

**ATT&CK:** T1110.001, T1078.003, T1005, T1041, T1053.003.

content.text: Identify protections and look for the comparison routine before brute force.

crackme-36: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, not stripped
    Arch:     amd64-64-little
    RELRO:    Full RELRO
    Stack:    No canary found
    NX:       NX enabled
    PIE:      PIE enabled
    Stripped: No

00000000000011a9 <check_password>:
    11a9:  endbr64
    11ad:  push   rbp
    11ae:  mov    rbp,rsp
    11b1:  mov    QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8],rdi
    11b5:  mov    rax,QWORD PTR [rbp-0x8]
    11b9:  movzx  eax,BYTE PTR [rax]
    11bc:  xor    eax,0x26
    11c2:  add    eax,0x3
    11c5:  cmp    al,BYTE PTR [rip+0x2e55]
    11cc:  jne    11e0 <check_password+0x37>
    ...
    11e0:  mov    eax,0x0
    11e5:  pop    rbp
    11e6:  ret
The check transforms each byte as `((c ^ key) + 3)` and compares it to a constant table. Dump the table and invert it in Python.

The comparison is a byte-wise `((input[i] ^ 0x26) + 3)` against a constant table in `.rodata`. Inverting the transform yields `nkh/zkyy/9C48`. The transform is reversible with the key embedded in the binary, so this is obfuscation, not protection.

content: Confirm the password locally and explain how to fix this design.

content.text: Run the lab binary once with the recovered argument to confirm, then write the design lesson.

Confirmed: `nkh/zkyy/9C48` is accepted and prints LAB{050aa77b}. **Fix:** never embed a reusable secret in a client-side binary. Move verification server-side, use a slow password hash (Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt) with a per-user salt, rate-limit attempts, and treat obfuscation as a speed bump only. If the binary must hold a key, use platform secure storage and rotate it.

CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-467). The lab service encrypts `attacker_input + secret` with
AES-128-ECB under a fixed unknown key and returns the ciphertext hex. Recover the secret
using the encryption oracle. The secret is a `LAB{...}` flag.

content.text: ECB encrypts identical 16-byte blocks identically. Confirm the block size and the presence of a repeated block after shifting the input.

A repeated block at 16 and 32 bytes confirms ECB and a 16-byte block size. Use the standard byte-at-a-time attack: align the secret so one unknown byte sits at the end of a block, then match the dictionary.

Recovered `LAB{aaeac217}`. ECB leaks equality: by shifting the input so each unknown byte lands at a known block position, the attacker builds a dictionary of ciphertext blocks and matches them one byte at a time. The attack needs only the encryption oracle.

content: What is the fix, and does adding a random prefix stop the attack?

content.text:
**Fix:** use a randomized AEAD mode (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with a fresh nonce per message. ECB is deterministic and should not be used for anything beyond a single fixed-size block with no attacker influence.

**Random prefix:** it raises the cost but does not stop the attack. The attacker can still locate the secret's block alignment by finding repeated blocks, then apply the same byte-at-a-time technique. It is not a security control; it is at best an obstacle.

The check transforms each byte as `((c ^ key) + 3)` and compares it to a constant table. Dump the table and invert it in Python.

content: Confirm the password locally and explain how to fix this design.

content.text: Run the lab binary once with the recovered argument to confirm, then write the design lesson.

Confirmed: `nkh/zkyy/6765` is accepted and prints LAB{09b6914e}. **Fix:** never embed a reusable secret in a client-side binary. If the binary must hold a key, use platform secure storage and rotate it.

SSRF is confirmed: the proxy can reach loopback (192.0.2.4:8081) and the cloud metadata service. The GCE metadata server is reachable and returns the default service-account token. The proxy returned the response body to an unauthenticated caller. I did not use the credentials; the impact is proven by the token response.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** a GCP access token for the instance's default service account. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** block metadata.google.internal and 169.254.169.254, require the Metadata-Flavor header at the proxy, and remove the default service account from the instance.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** temporary AWS credentials for the web tier's instance role; blast radius depends on that role. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** enforce IMDSv2 (token-required), scope the instance role to the reporting bucket prefix, add egress controls, and block link-local destinations at the application layer.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

content:
CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-259). The lab service encrypts `attacker_input + secret` with
AES-128-ECB under a fixed unknown key and returns the ciphertext hex. Recover the secret
using the encryption oracle. The secret is a `LAB{...}` flag.

content.text: ECB encrypts identical 16-byte blocks identically. Confirm the block size and the presence of a repeated block after shifting the input.

A repeated block at 16 and 32 bytes confirms ECB and a 16-byte block size. Use the standard byte-at-a-time attack: align the secret so one unknown byte sits at the end of a block, then match the dictionary.

Recovered `LAB{03cacbba}`. ECB leaks equality: by shifting the input so each unknown byte lands at a known block position, the attacker builds a dictionary of ciphertext blocks and matches them one byte at a time. The attack needs only the encryption oracle.

content: What is the fix, and does adding a random prefix stop the attack?

content.text:
**Fix:** use a randomized AEAD mode (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with a fresh nonce per message. ECB is deterministic and should not be used for anything beyond a single fixed-size block with no attacker influence.

**Random prefix:** it raises the cost but does not stop the attack. The attacker can still locate the secret's block alignment by finding repeated blocks, then apply the same byte-at-a-time technique. It is not a security control; it is at best an obstacle.

CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-214). The lab service encrypts `attacker_input + secret` with
AES-128-ECB under a fixed unknown key and returns the ciphertext hex. Recover the secret
using the encryption oracle. The secret is a `LAB{...}` flag.

content.text: ECB encrypts identical 16-byte blocks identically. Confirm the block size and the presence of a repeated block after shifting the input.

A repeated block at 16 and 32 bytes confirms ECB and a 16-byte block size. Use the standard byte-at-a-time attack: align the secret so one unknown byte sits at the end of a block, then match the dictionary.

Recovered `LAB{df06f85a}`. ECB leaks equality: by shifting the input so each unknown byte lands at a known block position, the attacker builds a dictionary of ciphertext blocks and matches them one byte at a time. The attack needs only the encryption oracle.

content: What is the fix, and does adding a random prefix stop the attack?

Recovered `LAB{d7e8b652}`. ECB leaks equality: by shifting the input so each unknown byte lands at a known block position, the attacker builds a dictionary of ciphertext blocks and matches them one byte at a time. The attack needs only the encryption oracle.

Engagement ENG-2026-689 — authorized test of http://files.lab.local (172.16.20.208).
`/fetch?url=` proxies a user-supplied URL. Determine whether it can reach internal
services (SSRF), read-only. Do not fetch customer data or use any credentials found.

content.text: Baseline the proxy with a documented internal health endpoint, then test loopback and link-local.
Loopback works. Test the cloud metadata endpoint next, but only read identity metadata.

SSRF is confirmed: the proxy can reach loopback (172.16.20.9:8081) and the cloud metadata service. AWS IMDSv1 is reachable and returns temporary role credentials for `web-prod-role`. The proxy returned the response body to an unauthenticated caller. I did not use the credentials; the impact is proven by the token response.

content: What is the blast radius, and how do you fix it at the application and cloud layers?

content.text: Separate application controls from cloud/network controls and add detection.

**Blast radius:** temporary AWS credentials for the web tier's instance role; blast radius depends on that role. Internal-only HTTP services are also reachable, so an attacker can pivot to admin panels and service discovery endpoints.

**Application fix:** parse the URL, allowlist scheme/host/port, resolve DNS and reject private, loopback, link-local, and multicast ranges *after* resolution, disable redirects, and re-check on every redirect hop. Do not rely on a string blocklist.

**Cloud fix:** enforce IMDSv2 (token-required), scope the instance role to the reporting bucket prefix, add egress controls, and block link-local destinations at the application layer.

**Detection:** alert on URLs containing `169.254.169.254`, `metadata.google.internal`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, decimal/hex IP encodings, and on metadata API calls from application hosts. Rotate any credential that may have been exposed.

content: Would a DNS allowlist alone be sufficient? Explain the bypasses.

content.text: No. A DNS allowlist can be bypassed by DNS rebinding (the first resolution is public, the second is private), redirects, IPv6-mapped IPv4 (`::ffff:127.0.0.1`), decimal/octal/hex IP forms, and alternate metadata hostnames. You need to resolve once, validate every resolved address, pin the connection to that IP (or revalidate immediately before connect), disable redirects, and enforce the same policy at the network egress layer. Treat the allowlist as one layer, not the control.

content.text:
**Remediation:** do not build a shell string from user input. Use an argument vector (`subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], shell=False)`), validate `host` as an IP or an allowlisted hostname, enforce a destination allowlist, drop capabilities, run in a read-only container, and remove secrets from the web root.

content:
CTF crypto task (ENG-2026-747). `cipher.txt` contains a base64 blob encrypted with
a repeating XOR key (lowercase letters, 4-7 chars). Recover the flag and explain
why this construction is weak.

content.text: Decode the blob, infer the key length from repeating patterns, then recover the key using the known `flag=` prefix.

The repeating XOR key is `llkzks` and the plaintext is `flag=LAB{06c31d4d}`. Known-plaintext (`flag=`) plus the short key length makes this recoverable in seconds; XOR also preserves language statistics, so frequency analysis works even without a known prefix.

content: Explain the fix and how to detect weak crypto in code review.

content.text:
**Fix:** use authenticated encryption with a random nonce — AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 — and a key from a KMS/secret manager. Never reuse a nonce with GCM. For password storage, use Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt, not encryption.

**Code-review detection:** grep for `chr(ord(` / `^` loops over data, `base64` used as “encryption”, hard-coded key bytes, `Cipher.getInstance("AES/ECB", ...)`, and `Random()` for keys. Add a SAST rule and a dependency policy for vetted crypto libraries.
